title: Account of Studying Abroad at the University of Warwick
paragraphs: The Nagoya University School of Medicine has a study abroad program in which, in the final year, students go overseas for about three months, take part in clerkships among local medical students, and study clinical medicine. Since entering the university I had been interested in how medicine is studied overseas and what kind of lives overseas medical students lead, and as I gathered information I thought that it looked hard but I would apply. Because I had lived in Toronto, Canada, for about three years as an elementary school child, and because I might study for a US medical license in the future, I first aimed at American universities. However, my TOEFL score, a requirement for applying, stagnated, and many of my friends also wanted the United States, so I thought it might not be possible. As a result of the selection meeting, it was decided that I would study at the University of Warwick in England. Embarrassingly, at that time my knowledge of England was limited to the Harry Potter films, and I was anxious about whether the food and environment would suit me. But since I would be going as a representative of Nagoya University's medical students, I needed to make my resolve and purpose clear. At present the common language of medicine worldwide is English, and polishing medical English from the student years is not a bad choice. In addition, I had studied a little medical English alongside my clinical clerkships in Japan, so I also felt like making use of that. Since I was going to a country I did not know at all, I also wanted to broaden my values with a hungry attitude.

Even after it was decided that I would go, it was hard. I could not get replies from the local university even when I contacted them, so I tried contacting them by international call, and when I was really in trouble, I was helped by Associate Professor 粕谷 of the International Collaboration Office. Also, I was told that, for a short stay of three months, the university could not arrange a dormitory, so I had to look for a place to live by myself, and I was frustrated by the complexity of the procedures for the UK visa application. Looking back, I think the preparation stage for studying abroad was itself very good English study.

The first thing I felt upon arriving was that it was far too cold. Early spring in England is usually pleasant, they say, but that year a cold wave that comes once in fifty years arrived. In Japan the cherry blossoms had begun to bloom, but in London there was sideways-blowing snow. If you go north for about an hour on a high-speed train, you arrive at a small town called Coventry. When I finally reached the house, the caretaker and landlord, a Scottish-descended Briton, welcomed me. However, he was extremely frugal and turned off the heating and the lights in the room at 10 p.m. Since I was being allowed to live there, I could not protest strongly. I will probably never again sleep wearing all the clothes I brought and a scarf. I also learned that people from the north of England have such strong dialects that they are extremely hard to understand. In the end, even after three months, when I encountered an unfamiliar dialect I could not understand at all.

While I was facing inconveniences different from those in Japan, the clerkship went along smoothly. Professor Singer, who was the contact point for the University of Warwick medical school, was truly a British gentleman, and when I consulted him about things I did not understand or was troubled by during the clerkship, he responded and solved them immediately even though he was busy.

The first department I was assigned to was radiology. There are 23 consultants, who correspond to what are called supervising doctors in Japan, and about 10 registrars in training, who handle work such as reading X-rays and CT, IVR, radiation therapy and ultrasound examinations. I was very surprised that when reading images, most of the doctors made their reading reports with voice recognition using a microphone. Will we also come to work with microphones in Japan before long? I was allowed to take part in IVR, to perform ultrasound examinations, and to attend MDT meetings held jointly with other departments. The professor of radiology was a very caring teacher, and I think I was able to have an educational clerkship.

Next I went to the department of diagnostic pathology. The supervising doctor in charge specialised in skin and respiratory pathology. I looked into the microscope together with the doctor and first stated the findings I could understand. On the first day of the clerkship, when I said that a skin slide had a lot of pigmentation, I was answered with a smile, "Indeed. Probably a Black person, I'd say," and I strongly felt the difference from Japan. At the weekly case conference, the registrars think about the educational cases prepared by the senior doctors, going back and forth over this and that, to search for the answer. The cases were so complicated that I was made aware that my level in both medical English and medical knowledge was far too low, and that frankly I could not keep up. In my free time I skimmed through morphology textbooks and absorbed words one by one, even if only roughly. On the last day of the clerkship I was given a summary, "You worked hard, you've grown quite a lot," which reassured me a little.

After the pathology assignment, I was supposed to rotate through emergency medicine, but it seemed the local trainees already filled it, so I decided to study in radiology once more. When I rotated before, the content was mostly going around the various examinations, but since I am interested in image reading, I volunteered to practice reading images. I was allowed a very luxurious clerkship in which I was given tasks such as X-ray, CT and MRI by day or by week, reported my findings and questions in the evening, and received feedback from the professor of radiology.

As an overall impression of the clerkships, in England medical students have a great deal of freedom in the content of their clerkships, there are many one-to-one situations with the doctors, and even a Japanese person can ask questions without hesitation, so I think I was able to learn enjoyably. I also had a lot of interaction with local students. I was asked what the factors behind Japan having the longest average life expectancy in the world might be, and we discussed it half jokingly, and we also talked about why many Asians cannot hold alcohol well. I interacted a lot with medical students from Malaysia and India and with students from other faculties, and we also went out for drinks.

One thing stays in my memory. It is a conversation with one of the radiology consultants. When I asked, aware of the rudeness, "Have you never thought of going to America? There is no language barrier, and I think America is an advanced country in medicine," he replied, "It is true that American doctors are paid better than in England, and on the strength of abundant funds they undoubtedly lead the world in the field of research. I honestly think it is impressive. But when I visited an American hospital, I got a cold impression, like 'if you don't have money, we won't treat you.' I wanted to become a doctor who treats not for money but simply because I want to cure." I was very surprised, because I had unconsciously imagined that excellent doctors around the world mostly go to America and build their careers. I felt I had caught a glimpse of the pride of working as a doctor in England.

Finally, I would like to close my account of studying abroad by expressing my great gratitude to everyone at the International Collaboration Office and the Academic Affairs Division who supported this study abroad, the seniors who taught us in the pre-departure training, my fellow exchange students who supported and encouraged each other, and all the people I met, starting with the local doctors.
